entries.title: Nvidia shareholders sue Jensen Huang over alleged spy ties
entries.summary: Nvidia shareholders have sued the chipmaker and its CEO, Jensen Huang, over his alleged ties to a suspected Chinese spy. The case adds to scrutiny over whether sensitive information at the AI giant was compromised.
entries.content:
November 10, 2026

Nvidia shareholders have sued the chipmaker and its CEO, Jensen Huang, over his alleged ties to a suspected Chinese spy. The case adds to scrutiny over whether sensitive information at the AI giant was compromised.

Shareholders sued chipmaker Nvidia and its chief executive, Jensen Huang, on Monday, accusing them of concealing his alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.

The proposed class action adds to investigations into whether Huang was targeted by foreign intelligence, raising questions about the security of sensitive information at the world's most valuable chipmaker.

What does the lawsuit allege?

The complaint, filed in federal court in San Jose, California, alleges that Nvidia and Huang misled investors about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who is not related to him.

Shareholders say the defendants failed to disclose national security concerns that threatened Nvidia's reputation and business prospects. They are seeking unspecified damages.

The New York Times reported last month on the alleged relationship and said US authorities had concluded that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset.

What have Nvidia and Huang said?

Nvidia announced an independent investigation Sunday into reports that Huang had been the "target of a foreign intelligence effort."

Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in an open letter, but did not identify the woman.

"I support the investigation and will cooperate fully," he said. "I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security."

Nvidia shares closed down 4.3% Monday. The lawsuit was filed five minutes after US markets closed.

How have Washington and Beijing responded?

US President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI was investigating the matter, while expressing support for Huang.

Trump said he had spoken to the executive earlier that day.

"He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy," Trump told reporters.

China denied conducting an intelligence operation targeting Huang.

"The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

Why does the case matter for the AI industry?

Huang co-founded Nvidia and led its transformation from a maker of gaming chips into a leading supplier of the computing technology powering artificial intelligence.

Its advanced chips have become a focus of US-China competition, with Washington restricting exports to limit Beijing's access to the technology.

Huang has pushed for looser restrictions on sales to China. The investigations have intensified scrutiny of his leadership and whether confidential company information was compromised.

entries.title: New trilateral talks on Ukraine war in Abu Dhabi: What to expect?
entries.summary: Ukrainian and Russian representatives last met in February for talks on ending the war, but the same sticking points remain. Ukraine continues to demand security guarantees, which is a non-starter for Russia.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine, Russia and US return to talks in Abu Dhabi: What to expect?

November 10, 2026

Ukrainian and Russian representatives last met in February for talks on ending the war, but the same sticking points remain. Ukraine continues to demand security guarantees, which is a non-starter for Russia.

A new round of trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraineand the United States are scheduled to take place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, months after a flurry of US-mediated peace talks earlier this year in January and February went nowhere.

When announcing the new trilateral talks last week, US special envoy Steve Witkoff said the discussions would focus on "post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has named security guarantees, an energy ceasefire, unblocking the Black Sea, extended prisoner exchanges, and preparations for a meeting of the leaders of Ukraine, the United States and Russia as his key topics.

Lawmaker Davyd Arakhamia, a member of Ukraine's delegation, told DW he was not expecting quick progress.

"I don't think there will be a breakthrough, after there was such a long break in the negotiation process," he said. "Simply the fact that trilateral talks are being resumed can be counted as a success."

Who is sitting at the table?

Witkoff will be joined by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, real estate developer Jared Kushner, who serves as special envoy. 

The Kremlin has sent Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin, to act as chief negotiator, along with a delegation including high-ranking Russian military and intelligence officials. 

The Ukrainian delegation will be led by Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, along with Arakhamia, and diplomatic and military officials.

Europe joins in

Separate formats are planned with several European representatives.

These include Günter Sautter, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's foreign and security policy adviser, Emmanuel Bonne, head of the Elysee Palace's diplomatic service and Jonathan Powell, the UK's national security advisor, and Fabrizio Saggio, diplomatic adviser to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

Björn Seibert, Chief of Staff for the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and Geoffrey van Leeuwen, Chief of Staff for NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, will also attend.

It's doubtful, however, whether European representatives will be formally involved in talks on a potential peace deal. 

Hanna Shelest, a security studies director at the foreign policy network Ukrainian Prism, told DW she believed they'd play "an observing role, at best."

She added that, until now, Russia had been reluctant to have European representatives at the table to uphold the impression that talks were "a matter between two superpowers" — namely, Russia and the United States — and to increase pressure on Washington.

"I doubt the Russian delegation will let the Europeans have a say," she told DW.

"Experience from the past years has taught us that as soon as Medinsky heads negotiations, the point becomes demonstrating to the US that Russia is willing to talk, but in reality, they won't reach an agreement," she explained. "Instead, there will be a long sermon about history and all sorts of other things."

However, she said Moscow sending high-ranking intelligence officers as part of the delegation was a "fairly positive aspect" of Russia's intentions.

She believed that additional negotiations were possible at this level.

This could include over prisoner exchanges or humanitarian pauses in villages near Oleshky, a town in the Russian occupied Kherson region in Ukraine's south, where US First Lady Melania Trump was credited with arranging a temporary truce in late October that secured humanitarian aid and allowed civilians to evacuate.

But despite these "positive signals," Shelest cautioned against hoping for concrete results, and suspected Russia was using the talks to stall.

Oleshky truce as a template for wider ceasefire?

Late last week, Trump spoke of a "big beautiful agreement," after speaking with Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev, "that might involve all of Europe."

This new security architecture, Kushner later clarified on social media, would be centered around "permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability."

These points "don't contain anything the Russians haven't been talking about since 2009," Shelest said.

Ivan Us, chief consultant and economic diplomacy expert at Ukraine's National Institute for Strategic Studies, pointed out that negotiations with people who are not decisions-makers could be simply for show.

But he agreed with other expert observers that negotiators in Abu Dhabi might try to use the temporary truce brokered for Oleshky as a model for other limited humanitarian ceasefires in the region.

But while Us said he saw cause for optimism, he also cautioned that Russia had continued attacks in Ukraine during the Oleshky truce, and had used the pause to fortify its positions around the town.

This article originally appeared in Ukrainian.

entries.title: Skydance replaces James Gunn and Peter Safran as DC Studios chiefs following Warner Bros. takeover
entries.summary: In another major shake-up for the DC Studios, Skydance is replacing Hollywood director James Gunn and producer Peter Safran with a former Marvel executive.
entries.content:
November 9, 2026

In another major shake-up for the DC Studios, Skydance is replacing Hollywood director James Gunn and producer Peter Safran with a former Marvel executive.

James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down as co-heads of DC Studios after four years, Skydance Motion Picture Group announced on Monday.

Their departure marks another major shake-up for the superhero franchise following Skydance's takeover of Warner Bros, just a year after Gunn's "Superman" reached cinemas.

Who will replace Gunn and Safran?

Skydance chairman and CEO David Ellison has chosen Jeremy Latchman, a former Marvel Studios executive, to lead DC Studios. He is set to become president and chief creative officer of DC Studios on December 1.

Latchman will oversee the next phase of DC's film and television business, which includes characters such as Superman, Batman and Wonder Woman.

He was involved in major Marvel productions including "Iron Man" and "The Avengers," and previously worked with Gunn and Safran on Marvel's "Guardians of the Galaxy" movie.

What did Gunn and Safran achieve?

Gunn and Safran took charge of DC Studios in 2022, tasked with rebuilding the franchise and creating a more unified cinematic universe.

Their first film, "Superman," earned nearly $619 million (€553 million) worldwide in 2025.

But their second release, "Supergirl," flopped in June 2026, taking around $126 million worldwide against a reported production budget of $170 million. The horror-inspired "Clayface" followed in October.

Overall, DC has struggled to match immense profits and cultural impact made by Marvel in the early years of its own cinematic universe.

"James and Peter launched a new era for DC Studios and led it through a period of real transformation, resetting the foundation and building a slate we're incredibly proud of," Ellison said in a statement.

"We're grateful for their passion, contributions and commitment to this legendary brand."

Gunn is currently completing "Man of Tomorrow," a sequel to "Superman." Other DC projects in development include "The Batman: Part II" and the television series "The People v. Gorilla Grodd."

Although Gunn and Safran will no longer oversee DC Studios' long-term plans, several projects developed under their leadership remain in production.

Was Gunn's Superman too 'woke' for conservatives?

Gunn's "Superman" sparked a political controversy in 2025 after the director described the superhero as an immigrant and emphasized themes of human kindness.

Conservative commentators accused the film of being "woke."

Skydance CEO Ellison has cultivated close ties with US President Donald Trump. Ellison has acknowledged having a good relationship with the administration but denied politicizing the company.

There is no evidence that the controversy surrounding "Superman" played a role in Gunn and Safran's replacement.

entries.title: US Pentagon chief Hegseth faces impeachment push over Iran war
entries.summary: Trump critic Thomas Massie is calling for a vote to impeach Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, accusing Hegseth of waging war without congressional approval.
entries.content:
United States of America

US Pentagon chief Hegseth faces impeachment push over Iran war

November 9, 2026

Trump critic Thomas Massie is calling for a vote to impeach Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, accusing Hegseth of waging war without congressional approval.

Republican lawmaker Thomas Massie, an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, introduced eight articles of impeachment against US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday as pressure builds on the Trump administration over the Iran war.

The resolution proposed by the Kentucky congressman accuses Hegseth of conducting the war illegally without congressional authorization. Massie also claims Hegseth has abused his powers as the head of the Pentagon.

Massie is using a special procedure that could see the US House of Representatives vote on the resolution within two days, with the legislative chamber still dominated by Republicans.

Trump told reporters at the White House that Hegseth had done a "good job" and had "won" wars in Venezuela and Iran.

"I'll stand by him... He won two wars. He was in charge," Trump said.

How has Hegseth responded?

Earlier on Monday, Hegseth sought to downplay rumors about the push against him.

"My team, we’re not worried about the noise," he told reporters.

Hegseth said he would hold a press conference Tuesday — his first in more than 180 days — and defended the war as necessary, even if unpopular.

Who supports impeachment?

Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries backed the effort Sunday.

"I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," he told ABC News. "Pete Hegseth has got to go."

Some Republicans have signaled they might support the charges. Arkansas congressman French Hill said he wanted to hear the debate before deciding.

The push follows Democrats' victories in both chambers of Congress in last week's midterm elections amid anger over the Iran war and soaring fuel prices. Republicans retain control until January 3.

Would impeachment remove Hegseth from office?

Impeachment requires a simple majority in the House and amounts to bringing formal charges. Removal would require a Senate trial and conviction by two-thirds of senators present.

Even with their enlarged majority next year, Democrats would need substantial Republican backing to reach that threshold.

entries.title: Pope Leo draws 2.5 million in Buenos Aires, renews warning over Milei's austerity
entries.summary: Some 2.5 million people have attended Pope Leo's mass in Buenos Aires, his largest gathering yet. The pontiff once again called for protecting the vulnerable as President Milei cuts disability care and social services.
entries.content:
Argentina

Pope Leo draws 2.5 million to Argentina mass, warns against austerity

November 9, 2026

Some 2.5 million people have attended Pope Leo's mass in Buenos Aires, his largest gathering yet. The pontiff once again called for protecting the vulnerable as President Milei cuts disability care and social services.

An estimated 2.5 million people attended Pope Leo XIV's open-air mass in Buenos Aires on Monday, according to local authorities, making the event the largest gathering of his papacy so far.

Crowds stretched for miles along Avenida del Libertador in Argentina's capital, with the faithful waving Vatican flags and chanting "Long live Pope Leo!" as the US-born pope passed in an open-top popemobile.

"It fills my heart with joy to celebrate... with you," Leo said in his sermon.

The pope also reinforced an appeal to President Javier Milei to protect vulnerable Argentines, visiting a disability care home struggling with the government's cuts to health care and social services.

What did Pope Leo say about Milei's spending cuts?

Before the mass, Leo visited the Cottolengo Don Orione care center in Claypole, south of Buenos Aires, which houses more than 400 people with disabilities.

He told residents their lives were a blessing rather than a burden, and challenged the idea that economic success alone measures a country's achievements.

"A nation's progress is also measured by how it welcomes all people with disabilities and particular needs," he said.

The remarks followed his appeal Sunday, at a reception attended by Milei, for economic growth to benefit people facing the greatest difficulties. He also urged leaders to choose their words carefully and recognize the limits of their power.

Milei became the president of Argentina some three years ago, Since then, his government has cut disability services and resisted implementing a law increasing funding for care, despite Congress overriding Milei's veto in 2025. The Senate is due to consider next year's disability funding in the coming days.

Argentina declares national holiday over Pope Leo's visit

Some worshippers camped overnight to secure a place near the Monumento a los Espanoles, where Pope John Paul II celebrated Argentina's last papal mass in 1987.

Monday was declared a national holiday to allow people to attend. President Milei and his sister Karina were among those present.

In his sermon, Leo spoke of families facing unstable employment, violence and addiction, while describing them as a pillar of society.

Where is the pope traveling next?

The visit is Argentina's first by a pope in nearly four decades. Leo's predecessor Francis, despite being born in Argentina, never returned to his homeland during his papacy.

Leo, 71, visited Uruguay before arriving in Argentina on Sunday. He is due to travel to Peru on Wednesday and return to Rome on November 17.

The first US-born pope spent decades in Peru as a missionary and bishop. The Vatican has described his South American tour as a "homecoming."

The demanding trip comes less than a month after surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his lung.

entries.title: French officials blame Iran for supermarket fridge hacking
entries.summary: The recent cyberattack on refrigerators and freezers in supermarkets in France was organized by Iran's Revolutionary Guards, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot has said, describing the hacking as "unprecedented."
entries.content:
France

French officials blame Iran for supermarket fridge hacking

November 9, 2026

The recent cyberattack on refrigerators and freezers in supermarkets in France was organized by Iran's Revolutionary Guards, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot has said, describing the hacking as "unprecedented."

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the attacks on French supermarkets last month came from Iran, and were carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), the elite branch of Iran's armed forces that answers directly to its religious leadership. 

"This attack is unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression," Barrot said, adding "we will implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack."

What happened during the alleged refrigeration cyberattack?

While the cyberattack was comparatively simple, it nevertheless had serious consequences for hundreds of supermarkets, spoiling large quantities of produce and in some cases setting temperatures so high that refrigeration units caught fire.

It was launched overnight on October 11-12, affecting around 700 of France's roughly 10,000 supermarkets.

A series of similar incidents also affected French supermarkets last week, and authorities even reported a failed attempt to hack cooling units at blood banks. 

Supermarkets in other European countries have reported similar security breaches, as have US authorities. It was not clear if any of all of these instances were connected.

What did French prosecutors say about the case?

Meanwhile, a Paris prosecutor provided details on the hacking probe:

"A judicial investigation has been opened against the head of the Iranian group Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit affiliated with the Electronic and Cyber Center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, against his two deputies, and against any other individuals who may be identified," Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said.

Barrot's Foreign Ministry said that France "condemns in the strongest possible terms the unacceptable cyberattacks carried out on its territory by the Islamic Republic of Iran."

entries.title: Russia: Independent Novaya Gazeta shuts its Moscow newsroom
entries.summary: The investigative newspaper is closing its doors after Russian authorities labeled it a "foreign agent" and ordered it vacate its Moscow premises.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Russia: Independent Novaya Gazeta shuts its Moscow newsroom

November 9, 2026

The investigative newspaper is closing its doors after Russian authorities labeled it a "foreign agent" and ordered it vacate its Moscow premises.

The Novaya Gazeta newspaper closed its Moscow office on Monday, saying it was not able to continue reporting amid a campaign of state pressure in Russia. 

The investigative outlet, co-founded by late USSR chief Mikhail Gorbachev, had long been a thorn in the Kremlin's side. In recent years, it ran into increasing roadblocks amid its critical coverage of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. 

It was branded a "foreign agent," a Soviet-era term resuscitated by President Vladimir Putin's administration, with officials ordering it to vacate its Moscow offices.

Russian banks were also forbidden from processing donations from readers and supporters. The paper had been heavily dependent on this income stream after moving wholly into online publishing, with the transition taking place shortly after the invasion of Ukraine. Russian authorities introduced new wartime censorship rules in the wake of the full-scale invasion.

Nobel Prize winner Muratov calls for free speech

2021 Nobel Peace Prize-winning founding editor Dmitry Muratov issued an appeal for free speech in wartime Russia as journalists gathered in the Novaya Gazeta offices to witness its closure. 

"Those in our country who advocate for peace have been denied the right to read what they choose, as we see happening today," he said. "We are currently at a point where the section of the Russian constitution that guarantees political and civil rights has ceased to function."

Russia's government meanwhile sought to play down the significance of the closure, with Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying it was part of a "rotational process" in a fiercely competitive media landscape.

What is Novaya Gazeta?

Novaya Gazeta was a flagship for post-Soviet democratic Russia and the era of "glasnost" or openness, also launched by Mikhail Gorbachev. The reformist Soviet leader used some of the prize fund for his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize as seed money for the publication.

The paper has built a reputation for fearless reporting, which has also put it in the crosshairs of Russia's wealthy and powerful. Six of its journalists were murdered since the paper was launched in 1993.

They included Anna Politkovskaya, who spent years investigating allegations of abuses by Russia's military during its campaigns in Chechnya. An early critic of Putin, she was found dead in her apartment bloc on the president's birthday in 2006. 

Images published in Russian media on Monday showed the paper's editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, taking down photographs of Polikovskaya and other reporters murdered in what's thought to be retribution for their work.

Last month, when first announcing that the paper would close, Sokolov said the outlet had "been killed." The paper was shutting down after "the Russian authorities — the Russian special services — have forced the editorial team to end its work," he said.

Will closure in Moscow mark a definitive end?

Muratov called for a ceasefire in Ukraine and urged foreign observers to remember the strength of dissent that endured in Russia, even if it was being pushed underground by censorship laws and other repression or intimidation.

"We canot blame the citizens themselves for this," Muratov said, "especially the wonderful, truly remarkable younger generation."

"I urge you to distinguish between the Russian authorities and the Russian people," he added.

Muratov also called for the release of around 4,000 people he termed political prisoners in Russia.

Novaya Gazeta's leadership has not made it entirely clear whether its closing down in Moscow marks a definitive end to the outlet's reporting, or whether they might perhaps seek to regroup and begin operating in some form from outisde Russia, as several other publications including DW have been forced to in recent years.

One of its journalists, Irina Vorobyova, said that the paper's spirit would survive like a "good virus" and would "continue in everyone that was part of it."

entries.title: India’s demonetization: 10 years on, promises remain unfulfilled
entries.summary: A decade after the 2016 currency ban, its impact on India's economy and the fight against black money remains contested.
entries.content:
India

India's demonetization: 10 years on, promises remain unfulfilled

November 9, 2026

A decade after the 2016 currency ban, its impact on India's economy and the fight against black money remains contested.

On November 8, 2016, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced in a televised address to the nation that he was withdrawing all 500- and 1,000-rupee banknotes from circulation at midnight.

The surprise move invalidated 86.9% of the value of currency in circulation in a single stroke.

Modi asked Indians to make a "grand sacrifice for cleansing our country."

He promised that the hardship would help eliminate black money, corruption, counterfeit currency and terrorist financing. The exercise was presented as a major step towards a cleaner and more transparent economy.

The cost to the informal economy

Millions of Indians rushed to banks to exchange their savings. Long queues formed outside banks and ATMs, with people waiting for hours, sometimes without knowing when they would get their money.

Workers missed wages, small businesses struggled to pay employees and families found it difficult to buy everyday essentials. Reports of people dying during the cash crisis added to the distress.

"I still remember my domestic help's father," businessman Prakash Patra from Jaipur city told DW. "He panicked, collapsed, and passed away right there, standing in a long queue just trying to exchange his family's life savings. It wasn't just cash that was lost in those lines. It was human lives."

For India's most vulnerable, particularly rural women and people without bank accounts, the sudden cash shortage made savings difficult to access. Money set aside for family weddings, medical emergencies and basic survival was suddenly compromised.

Joe Athialy, executive director of the New Delhi-based Center for Financial Accountability, a financial watchdog, says the impact fell disproportionately on the poor and the informal economy.

"Demonetization destroyed livelihoods, disrupted small businesses and pushed millions into deeper economic insecurity. The poor and those dependent on the informal sector bore the greatest cost," Athialy told DW.

Arun Kumar, former professor of economics at Jawaharlal Nehru University and author of "The Black Economy in India," shared a similar assessment. The government wrongly assumed that illicit wealth was primarily held in cash, he said.

"And it penalized the cash-dependent informal sector while leaving the real engines of the black economy untouched," Kumar told DW.

Did it solve the black money problem?

The first major setback came in 2018, when the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) reported that 99.3% of the demonetized currency had returned to the banking system.

Only a small fraction of the withdrawn money had failed to come back, undermining the expectation that large amounts of undeclared cash would be extinguished.

A decade later, there is little evidence that demonetization made a significant dent in black money or corruption. Economists have long pointed out that much illicit wealth in India is held in property, gold and other assets rather than cash.

Some supporters of the policy argued that forcing cash into the banking system would help formalize the economy and widen the tax base. But the extent to which these changes could be attributed to the currency withdrawal remains contested.

Lekha Chakraborty, a professor at the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy, said research after the exercise pointed to limited success in achieving its stated objectives.

She draws on studies that examined both the immediate economic shock and its longer-term effects.

"The research points to modest gains against demonetization's primary objectives, alongside temporary but real economic costs. The impact was particularly severe in the informal sector, where cash remains central to everyday transactions," Chakraborty told DW.

"The economic shock was real, even if much of it faded over time. But there is little to suggest that demonetization produced a lasting change in the way black wealth is generated or concealed."

Athialy argues that the policy was based on a flawed understanding of how illicit wealth is held in India.

"Cash is only an insignificant part of the black economy. Much of India's unaccounted wealth is held in assets such as real estate and in tax havens, not currency," he said.

He also questions the absence of accountability for the disruption and its institutional consequences.

"Nobody has been held accountable for the economic disruption or the undermining of institutions such as the RBI."

Boost to digital payments

Digital payments have expanded rapidly since 2016. The Unified Payments Interface (UPI), launched in August that year, has become a major part of India's retail payment system today.

In 2025-26, UPI processed 241.6 billion transactions, worth 314.2 trillion rupees (approximately €2.95 trillion), according to the RBI.

Yet the growth of digital payments has not reduced the amount of physical currency in circulation.

RBI data show that the value of banknotes in circulation stood at 43.15 trillion rupees (about €405 billion) on October 23, 2026, compared with 17.97 trillion rupees (€169 billion) in November 2016.

The figures show that Indians are increasingly using digital platforms for everyday payments, but cash remains firmly in circulation.

Chakraborty cautions against attributing the growth of digital payments to demonetization. "Digital payments largely continued a trend that was already under way before the currency ban," she said.

A decade after the unprecedented move, the gap between the government's promises and what demonetization ultimately delivered remains central to its legacy.

entries.title: Ice hockey: Norway says it's been kicked out of World Juniors in favor of Russia
entries.summary: The wrangling over Russia's return to international ice hockey continues, with Norway saying it has been kicked out of the next major tournament to accommodate Russia. Switzerland has joined a "boycott."
entries.content:
November 9, 2026

The wrangling over Russia's return to international ice hockey continues, with Norway saying it has been kicked out of the next major tournament to accommodate Russia. Switzerland has joined a "boycott."

With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th (of 10) participant. This comes after the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association (NIHF) said that the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had informed it that it had been removed from the tournament so that Russia could take part.

The move, which has yet to be publicly announced by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to last month's Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play. The World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the CAS decision. The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In a statement issued on Saturday, the IIHF said it was "taking the necessary steps required by the CAS ruling and reviewing what conditions would need to be met to safeguard our Championships, protect the organization's financial stability and secure the long-term future of international ice hockey."

As of Monday, the IIHF website still listed Norway as one of the participants in the World Juniors, which is to be hosted by Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta, beginning on December 26. Still, Swiss Ice Hockey responded to Norway's statement, saying its team would not face Russia at the World Juniors — as would be the case if it replaces Norway in the schedule.

However, it is far from certain that Russia will actually be able to ice a team in the tournament, as just last week, the Canadian prime minister ruled out the possibility.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," Mark Carney said.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."

How this circle could be squared is unclear. Carney's pledge, coupled with the stated refusal by Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and others to face Russia in an international tournament, appears to have given the NIHF hope that its team could still play in the upcoming World Juniors. Several long-time corporate sponsors have also threatened to pull out if Russia is allowed to compete.

"This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada in December," NIHF General Secretary Petter Salsten said.

"The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association is awaiting further information from the IIHF in the coming days."

Hosts Germany continue to explore options

Meanwhile, the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) is still in discussions with the government in Berlin and the IIHF about how to proceed — or not — with hosting the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship next May.

"We intend to host the World Championship in Germany next year, and I am very optimistic that we will succeed in doing so," DEB chairman Frank H. Lutz told German broadcaster MagentaSport on Saturday.

While he acknowledged the IIHF's CAS-ordered requirement to include Russia and reiterated the DEB's rejection of the court ruling, he provided no indication as to how this obstacle could be overcome.

Lutz, who said he would be in Berlin for more consultations this week, had previously said handing back Germany's hosting rights was a possibility — if only as a last resort.

On Friday, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin supports the DEB's efforts to find a solution.

"However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore, through dialogue, how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."

Asked at the same press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman indicated that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.

However, he did not categorically rule out the possibility.

Could Munich's Olympic bid be a factor?

It has been suggested that government officials could be choosing their words carefully out of concern for Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees who are bidding to host an Olympic Games — like the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) — to follow its lead.

Asked whether the debate over Russia's possible involvement in a hockey tournament could affect Munich's chances, government spokesman Kornelius said he didn't wish to "speculate on implications."

Still, with the IOC set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process, one has to think that the issue could hardly have come up at a more inopportune time for the DOSB.

entries.title: Fake news in Africa: In an age of disinformation, who decides what's true?
entries.summary: From Ghana to Mozambique, the fight against fake news keeps gaining momentum. But combating disinformation also requires safeguards for free speech, leaving some governments in an inconvenient position.
entries.content:
November 9, 2026

From Ghana to Mozambique, the fight against fake news keeps gaining momentum. But combating disinformation also requires safeguards for free speech, leaving some governments in an inconvenient position.

Misinformation poses a threat to democracy worldwide: An exaggerated WhatsApp message, a manipulated TikTok video or an apparent breaking news alert on Facebook can all misguide people in Africa and beyond — particularly in the run-up to elections.

As artificial intelligence is making it increasingly easy to manipulate images, voices and videos, more and more countries are trying to equip their populations with skills to identify and counter fake news.

But are these efforts really about raising awareness, or are certain governments using this fight to control public opinion, silence dissident voices and misguide the populace — from both within and outside of these respective nations?

Civil society groups fill gaps left by governments

Journalism lecturer Dani Madrid-Morales at the University of Sheffield believes that African governments must significantly step up their efforts to combat sources of disinformation and misinformation.

He told DW that "there are very few countries — if any — that are actually doing a good job" to beat the influence of fake news.

Meanwhile, he points out that there also are civil society initiatives in various African nations, which help inform people about the dangers of such false narratives.

For instance in South Africa, organizations like Africa Check and Media Monitoring Africa work together to highlight the impact of fake news on elections. Similar coalitions also exist in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Senegal.

However, these initiative mostly focus on fighting disinformation during election periods; the rest of the time, they typically lack funding and sustained engagement with civil society to continue to make a change.

When African governments become part of the problem

There also are deliberate efforts by certain governments not to battle fake news; some let it happen while others engage in deliberately spreading this kind of disinformation.

Madrid-Morales distinguishes between three types of disinformation in this context: There are scams and similar schemes, which some governments, he says, fail to sufficiently fight, leaving people susceptible to financial losses and other problems.

Secondly, he adds that there also are certain foreign influence operations trying to impact public opinion from outside a country and, in many instances, outside of the continent.

Finally, there are political disinformation campaings which originate from within a country that are intended to deliberately derail impartial views, he explains.

"Governments are particularly interested in the third category," says Madrid-Morales, adding that this is especially prevalent in the Sahel region.

He highlights how in nations like Burkina Faso and Mali, military governments have shut down media outlets, prosecuted journalists and expelled foreign correspondents in order to silence free speech.

In his view, these junta governments are primarily concerned with preventing negative or false information about themselves from circulating rather than actively recruiting followers.

Do outside forces shape public opinion in Africa?

Foreign powers meanwhile also appear to play a considerable role in shaping public opinion across the continent.

Afrobarometer, a pan-African research network, examined the influence of international actors in terms of their influence across Africa — including those suspected of sharing fake news.

The study found that over 60% of respondents viewed China's political and economic influence positively; this was followed by 52% for the United States.

Both countries have no past colonial history in Africa, although they are now competng for economic gains while focusing otherwise on furthering infrastructure projects — partly to maintain this largely benevolent perception towards them.

However, perceptions of other former colonial powers vary notably in some cases, depending mainly on factors such as the impact of past injustices: For example, in French-speaking countries, only 34% of respondents viewed France's ongoing influence positively.

Komi Amewonou from Afrobarometer  told DW that such attitudes are not necessarily the outcome of targeted propaganda campaigns for or against certain nations outside the continent but rather the result of African governments letting negative perceptions simply run their course.

The mixed role of media literacy initiatives

In some countries, there are media development project trying to educate people and animate them to think for themselves and thus fight sources of fake news and disinformation.

In Ghana, the NGO Penplusbytes runs the "Caravan of Hope" initiative — a project supported by the German development agency GIZ and by DW Akademie. 

This mobile campaign brings media literacy training to rural communities through theater, role-playing exercises, public discussions and videos in local languages. The initiative has managed to reach 3,000 people in five districts to date.

The campaign also involves trusted community figures, as studies show that locals most trust people they know personally — particularly traditional village leaders and community representatives.

Rebecca Avusu from Penplusbytes, who helped develop the project, told DW that "information must be verified before people believe it or pass it on. This is particularly important for those without smartphones or with limited formal education."

Initiatives in South Africa take a similar approach: The country is home to Africa Check — one of the continent's best-known fact-checking initiatives.

The organization visits schools and teaches classes how to identify manipulated images, verify sources, and deal with misinformation circulating on WhatsApp groups.

However, Madrid-Morales says that there can be a downside to such media literacy programs as well; pointing to research conducted in South Africa, he highlights that while some young people do become more discerning consumers of information, others eventually lose trust in almost every source, resulting in a complete lack of knowledge about important developments.

Limited powers elsewhere in Africa

In countries elsewhere in Africa, there's greater resistance against such media literacy initiaves — chiefly by their own governments.

In 2026, the International Media and Information Literacy Institute (IMILI) was opened in the Nigerian capital Abuja under the auspices of UNESCO, with a mission to promote research, training and international cooperation across media literacy initiatives.

This came after the Nigerian government announced that it aimed to play a leading international role in Africa in the fight against fake news; however, civil rights groups say the state often blurs the line between genuinely battling disinformation and silencing public dissent in the country.

In Kenya, there are similar concerns: The Media Council of Kenya has been tasked with supporting journalists and boosting fact-checking initiatives.

However, its scope of operations is limited, as the organization abides by the country's laws to remain in operation — in particular legislation supposedly designed to target the spreading of false information.

Conversely, these laws have come under increased scrutiny, as they can also be abused to silence views against the government.

Madrid-Morales says that in such contexts, there need to be independent oversight bodies to ensure that people do not refrain from expressing themselves publicly for fear of reprisal.

Mozambique: Fighting disinformation as a tool of control

Meanwhile in Mozambique, the media institute MISA has also launched a series of media initiatives such as MISACheck. The program is designed to train young journalists and social activists in fact-checking techniques.

Olivia Massango, the vice-president of MISA, says however that the efforts of such civil society groups may seem like a drop in the ocean; Massango is particularly critical of how state authorities deal with misinformation.

"When something becomes inconvenient, the government ... invokes public interest, but ultimately often ends up protecting only what suits it," she told DW.

"Combating disinformation must not mean criminalizing opinions, criticism or journalistic work," she warns.

Guidance from Europe — with limited safeguards

More and more African nations meanwhile are turning to Europe in hopes of adopting useful mechanisms to fight fake news.

Morocco and Senegal are among the examples where proposed disinformation legislation is widely inspired by EU standards. Madrid-Morales however stresses that while following strong EU legislation in the battle against disinformation can be a success, there also need to be independent oversight and enforcement mechanisms to make them work.

In the cases of Senegal and Morocco, these are yet to be established, he explains, stressing that both nations have repeatedly had to deal with various forms of political instability influenced by fake news.

Rebecca Avusu says she is also concerned about such efforts maintaining loopholes to suit governments if and as needed: "We do not want laws designed to combat disinformation to become instruments for silencing people who question government decisions or express legitimate opinions," Avusu warns.
